summary: Describes Sieve, a language for filtering email at final delivery on a client or server. It is simple and extensible, and it has no variables, loops, or ability to run external programs, so it is suitable for servers where users cannot run arbitrary code. It replaces RFC 3028. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Sieve is a short rulebook for sorting mail, like put newsletters in this folder. It is safe because the rules cannot run dangerous programs.

subtitle: A small, safe language for sorting incoming email by rules, with no loops, variables or shell access.

tldr.problem: Users want to filter mail at delivery time, but a server that runs user scripts must not let them run arbitrary programs.
tldr.mechanism: Sieve is a simple command language of tests and actions (if, header, address, fileinto, redirect, discard and others) with no variables, loops or external programs, plus a require mechanism for extensions.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 3028 and is a Proposed Standard that several later RFCs have updated.

today: RFC 5228 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3028. It has been updated by RFC 5229, RFC 5429, RFC 6785 and RFC 9042.

sections.title: What Sieve Is For
sections.content:
Sieve is a language for filtering email messages at the time of final delivery, when the message is moved to the user's mailbox. It is not tied to any operating system or mail architecture, but it requires messages in the Internet Message Format.

The language is powerful enough to be useful but deliberately limited so that a server can safely run users' scripts. The base language was not designed to be Turing-complete: it has no loops or functions, and no variables or way to run external programs. That makes it suitable even for "black box" IMAP servers where users cannot execute arbitrary code.

The authors note that experience at Carnegie Mellon showed many users filter mail when it is easy, and expect graphical editors to be the preferred way to write filters.
sections.eli5: Sieve is like a short list of sorting rules for your mailbox. It is simple on purpose, so nobody can sneak in anything dangerous.

sections.title: Scripts, Tokens and Data
sections.content:
A script is a sequence of commands. Each command is a name followed by arguments, which can be numbers, strings, string lists, tags, tests or blocks. Outside strings and comments the language is limited to US-ASCII, and strings are normally UTF-8. Tokens other than strings are case-insensitive.

  • Comments: a hash sign to the end of the line, or bracketed comments that open with a slash and an asterisk and close with the reverse, which do not nest.
  • Numbers: decimal, with an optional K, M or G suffix meaning 1,024, 1,048,576 or 1,073,741,824 times the value. Implementations MUST support 0 to 2,147,483,647.
  • Strings: quoted, or a multi-line form starting with text: and ending with a line holding a single period.
  • String lists: ["a", "b"]. A test matches if any string in the list matches, and a single string equals a one-item list.

Arguments come in three kinds: positional, tagged (beginning with a colon, such as :contains) and optional. Tagged arguments must come before positional ones. The formal grammar in the RFC is the authority on how to build commands, and it is deliberately loose so extensions need not change it.

The encoded-character extension lets a script write bytes or Unicode characters using only US-ASCII, as in ${hex:24 24} for two dollar signs. Using non-UTF-8 text in scripts is deprecated.
sections.eli5: A Sieve script is a list of short instructions written in plain text, a bit like a recipe card with if-this-then-that lines.

sections.title: Matching Strings
sections.content:
Tests that compare strings take an optional match type. :is needs an exact match and is the default, :contains matches a substring, and :matches is a wildcard match where the asterisk matches zero or more characters and the question mark matches one character, and the whole value must match.

A comparator, given with :comparator, decides how characters are compared. All implementations MUST support i;octet, which compares octets exactly, and i;ascii-casemap, which ignores case in the US-ASCII range. The default is i;ascii-casemap, and header names are always compared case-insensitively. Other comparators must be declared with require.

Tests on addresses can also take an address part: :localpart (left of the at-sign), :domain (right of it) or :all, the default. It is an error to give more than one match type, comparator or address part to one command.

Header text in other character sets is converted to UTF-8 before comparison, and implementations MUST be able to convert US-ASCII, ISO-8859-1 and UTF-8.
sections.eli5: You can ask whether a subject is exactly some words, contains some words, or fits a pattern with wildcards. You can also say whether capital letters count.

sections.title: Control, Actions and Tests
sections.content:
There are three kinds of command. Control commands shape the flow: if/elsif/else run exactly one block of a chain (or none), require declares extensions and MUST come before any other command, and stop ends processing. Blocks run once or not at all, so there are no loops.

Actions do things to the message. Implementations MUST support keep, discard and redirect, and SHOULD support fileinto. A redirect sends the message on as a mail forward would, must preserve existing Received headers and must keep an empty envelope sender empty to avoid loops. discard silently drops the message and MUST NOT send any non-delivery notice.

Tests are used in conditions. Implementations MUST support address, allof, anyof, exists, false, header, not, size and true, and SHOULD support envelope. allof is logical AND, anyof is logical OR, and size takes :over or :under with a limit, so a message of exactly 4,000 octets is neither over nor under 4000.

The header test ignores leading and trailing whitespace. A header that exists contains the empty key, but a missing header matches nothing. The envelope test checks the SMTP from or to envelope parts.
sections.eli5: Tests ask questions about a message, such as who sent it or how big it is. Actions say what to do, such as file it in a folder, forward it or throw it away.

sections.title: How a Script Runs
sections.content:
Scripts cannot cover every case, so Sieve has an implicit keep: if nothing files, redirects or discards the message, the normal keep happens anyway. Any of fileinto, keep, redirect or discard cancels it. The stop command still allows the implicit keep if it has not been cancelled.

Implementations SHOULD NOT deliver a message to the same mailbox twice even if asked, and that MUST NOT be treated as an error. Site policy MAY limit the number of actions, but implementations MUST allow at least one keep or one fileinto.

An extension not enabled with require must be treated as if unsupported. If a required extension is unavailable, no later command may run. When any error occurs, processing stops, the user is notified of the error and which actions were taken, and an implicit keep is performed. Implementations MUST support fifteen levels of nested blocks and fifteen levels of nested test lists.
sections.eli5: If none of your rules say what to do with a letter, it goes in your normal inbox. That way nothing gets lost by accident.

sections.title: Extensions and Capability Strings
sections.content:
New commands, tests and actions can be added. Each extension MUST define a case-sensitive capability string that scripts name in require. If a new version of an extension changes the functionality of an earlier one, it MUST use a different name. Extensions MUST say how they interact with the base actions, such as whether they cancel the implicit keep, and MUST NOT change how require works.

This RFC defines the capability strings encoded-character, envelope, fileinto and the comparator- prefix. Strings beginning with vnd. are vendor-defined and registered with IANA first-come, first-served. Other prefixes require a standards track or IESG-approved experimental RFC. The RFC does not define how a server advertises its supported extensions.

The MIME type for a script is application/sieve, with file extensions .siv and .sieve.
sections.eli5: If someone adds a new trick to the language, scripts must say up front that they use it, so nothing behaves in a surprising way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Scripts must be protected from unauthorized modification: an attacker who edits a script can cause mail to be discarded, rejected or forwarded to the wrong person. Scripts SHOULD also be protected from retrieval, since they may reveal mailbox names and correspondents' addresses. The RFC even warns that someone leaving a terminal logged in could have their script changed to just discard, so implementations MAY keep discarded messages for a while and MAY disallow scripts that throw away all mail.

redirect can be abused to flood a target or to multiply messages. Implementations therefore:

  • MUST detect and break message loops.
  • MUST let administrators limit how many redirects a script performs, and if multiple destinations are not needed, SHOULD set that limit to 1.
  • MUST be able to log redirect use.
  • MAY analyze scripts to judge whether they are safe to run.

If Sieve and the mail agents behind it interpret malformed messages differently, an attacker might subvert the filter.
sections.eli5: Because a rule can throw mail away or forward it, only you should be able to change your rules, and the server should stop anyone from using forwarding to flood someone.

data.title: Sieve control example

items.label: Keep
items.desc: Save the message in the default location, normally the main mailbox.

items.label: File into
items.desc: Deliver the message into a named mailbox. Implementations SHOULD support it.

items.label: Redirect
items.desc: Send the message on to another address, as mail forwarding does.

items.label: Discard
items.desc: Silently throw the message away by cancelling the implicit keep.
